records.title: Vitamin C and Methylprednisolone Modulate Apoptotic and Transcript Responses in a B-35 Scratch Screening Model.
records.abstract: In vitro mechanical injury platforms using proliferative neuronal cell lines provide accessible systems for preliminary pharmacological screening before progression to differentiated, primary, or in vivo models. We investigated the effects of vitamin C and methylprednisolone, alone or in combination, on cell viability, Annexin V/PI-defined apoptotic cell death, scratch-gap closure, and selected transcript responses in the B-35 rat neuroblastoma cell line. Mechanical injury was induced in confluent B-35 monolayers using a standardized scratch method. Vitamin C, methylprednisolone, or their combination was applied either immediately after injury (0 h) or after a 24 h delay. Scratch-gap closure was quantified by image-based analysis, and IL-4, IL-10, and TUBB3 expression was evaluated by quantitative real-time PCR. Early combined exposure to vitamin C and methylprednisolone was associated with low apoptotic cell fractions, faster scratch-gap closure, and higher IL-4, IL-10, and TUBB3 mRNA levels than either single treatment, whereas delayed treatment showed attenuated responses. These findings describe treatment-associated changes in a simplified B-35 cell-line screening model. They should not be interpreted as evidence of regeneration, pharmacological synergy, neuroprotection, or spinal cord injury therapy. Protein-level validation, proliferation control, and confirmation in differentiated neuronal cultures, primary neuronglia co-cultures, organoid or slice models, and in vivo injury systems are required before mechanistic or translational conclusions can be drawn.

records.title: Amcinonide Exhibits Antitumor Effects in Radioresistant Colorectal Cancer Through the circRNF10/miR-296-5p/Snail Axis.
records.abstract: Radiotherapy, commonly used in the treatment of colorectal cancer (CRC), can induce local recurrence and malignant progression in cases of intrinsic and acquired radioresistance; therefore, effective treatment strategies are required. In this study, we screened an FDA-approved drug library and identified amcinonide (AMC), a topical corticosteroid, as a potential agent that inhibits radiation-induced epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), cell migratory ability, and invasiveness in radioresistant colorectal cancer cells. Mechanistically, ionizing radiation-induced circRNF10 suppressed miR-296-5p, thereby increasing Snail expression and promoting EMT and aggressive phenotypes in radioresistant CRC cells. We verified in vitro, in vivo, and in CRC patient-derived organoids (PDOs) models that AMC suppresses the malignant phenotype by restoring miR-296-5p expression and reducing Snail expression. These findings identify the circRNF10/miR-296-5p/Snail axis as a key factor in CRC radioresistance and suggest that it may serve as a therapeutic target. Together, these results suggest that AMC is a promising drug for overcoming CRC radioresistance and that components of this axis may serve as potential diagnostic biomarkers. Overall, these findings highlight the therapeutic potential of targeting the ncRNA-mediated EMT circuit to overcome radioresistant CRC.

records.title: Human stem cell-based embryo models and the 2025 ISSCR Guidelines.
records.abstract: With the 2025 revisions to the ISSCR Guidelines for Stem Cell Research and Clinical Translation, human stem cell-based embryo models (SCBEMs) sit within a clearer governance framework. We argue, however, that four practical challenges require further clarification. First, specialized oversight of human SCBEM research could be delayed where integration-building work is distributed across several protocols. Second, ambiguity persists at the boundary between SCBEMs and stage- or structure-specific 3D constructs. Third, the new oversight standards for human SCBEM research are not explicitly linked to the ethical principles set out in the Guidelines. Finally, animal implantation or gestation findings could be accorded too much weight when committees consider the limits and scope of human SCBEM safeguards. In light of these four challenges, we propose four targeted clarifications: (1) a narrowly framed consultation trigger for defined protocol-level integration-building manipulations, without moving ordinary organoid, endometrial, placental, or trophoblast research into Category 2; (2) a Category 3B clarification distinguishing permissible, time-limited implantation modelling from impermissible attempts to enable sustained gestational or ectogenetic progression; (3) guidance limiting the decisive inferential use of animal SCBEM gestation evidence in human SCBEM oversight; and (4) a short note linking SCBEM classification and the ISSCR's ethically motivated limits on preclinical human SCBEM research to explicit criteria and ethical justification.

records.title: Coupling oxidative de-stabilization with immune activation overcomes radioresistance in hepatocellular carcinoma.
records.abstract: Radioresistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a coordinated adaptive state rather than failure of a single pathway, sustained by reinforced redox buffering and suppressed immune activation. Strategies that intensify radiation damage without disrupting this state have shown limited efficacy. We sought to determine whether radiosensitization can be achieved by destabilizing tumor oxidative homeostasis while restoring immune competence. A BSA-templated Fe/Mn nanoassembly incorporating the thiol-reactive agent RRX-001 and folate targeting (BFMR-FA) was developed as a multifunctional and MRI-visible platform. Its biological effects were evaluated across radioresistant cellular systems, organoids, and orthotopic tumor models. BFMR-FA shifts the redox equilibrium of tumor cells beyond a recoverable threshold. By depleting glutathione and suppressing the SLC7A11-GPX4 axis, it converts radiation-induced oxidative stress from a transient signal into sustained lipid peroxidation, resulting in convergent ferroptotic and apoptotic cell death. This transition is accompanied by the emergence of immunogenic stress signals and activation of the STING-TBK1-IRF3 pathway, enabling dendritic cell maturation and expansion of cytotoxic T-cell responses. In vivo, these effects translate into near-complete suppression of radioresistant tumor growth with systemic tolerance. The Fe/Mn composition enables direct visualization of intratumoral delivery by T1-weighted MRI. These findings support a model in which radiosensitization is achieved not by amplifying tumor damage alone, but by collapsing the adaptive redox state that constrains it. The resulting oxidative destabilization coupled with immune activation defines an oxidative homeostasis collapse-driven radio-immuno synergy, providing a generalizable framework for overcoming therapeutic resistance in solid tumors.

records.title: Comparative characterization of OncoPro™ and Wnt-based media reveals distinct phenotypic and pharmacologic states in patient-derived tumor organoids.
records.abstract: Patient-derived tumor organoids (PDTOs) are strongly influenced by culture medium. We compared OncoPro™ (OP) Tumoroid Culture medium with conventional Wnt/R-spondin/noggin (Wnt) medium. This recently developed OP medium offers a standardized, serum-free alternative to Wnt-based formulations. We compared OP and Wnt media across 36 PDTO lines from various malignancies (colorectal, pancreatic, breast, lung, gastric, gastroesophageal junction, biliary head and neck and unknown primary), assessing establishment success. Selected PDTO models were subjected to downstream characterization, including morphological assessment and bulk transcriptomic profiling with comparison to public single-cell RNA sequencing reference datasets (n = 11), whole-exome sequencing (WES) (n = 9), and pharmacological response profiling to a 33-drug panel (n = 3). Adaptation from Wnt medium to OP succeeded in 83.3% (15/18), whereas de novo establishment favored Wnt (33.3% vs 11.1%). Key oncogenic driver alterations were retained across matched organoid cultures, supporting preservation of tumor-relevant genomic features. Transcriptomic profiling confirmed preserved tumor-identity across media, while revealing different epithelial state programs: Wnt upregulated proliferation/stemness-associated genes (e.g. LGR5) and OP enriched adhesion-associated genes and inflammatory/TGF-β programs. In scRNA databases OP signatures preferentially mapped to malignant epithelial compartments in pancreatic cancer, whereas Wnt signatures were linked to non-malignant epithelium. Similarly, in colon cancer OP signature mapped predominantly to the malignant epithelial compartments. Drug (n = 33) screening in pancreatic- and colorectal cancer PDTOs (n = 3) demonstrated consistent medium-dependent shifts: Wnt-grown PDTOs were globally more sensitive in the screened subset, particularly to MAPK-axis inhibitors and apoptosis-sensitizers, while OP-grown PDTOs exhibited relative resistance. Culture medium composition is a key determinant of PDTO phenotype, transcriptome and drug sensitivity. Wnt medium was associated with drug-sensitive states, whereas OP medium was associated with adhesion- and inflammatory-related programs, relative resistance in the screened subset of 33 drugs and closer alignment with malignant epithelial programs in the analyzed pancreatic / colorectal cancer single-cell atlases.

records.title: Early detection of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma via a CACNA1E-SNTG1 cfDNA methylation signature.
records.abstract: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) is characterized by high mortality primarily due to late-stage diagnosis. While circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) methylation offers a promising avenue for non-invasive screening, achieving high diagnostic sensitivity for early-stage disease using scalable clinical assays remains a technical challenge. This study aimed to identify robust methylation biomarkers and validate their diagnostic performance and biological relevance using a liquid biopsy approach and patient-derived models. Differentially methylated regions were identified through whole-genome enzymatic methyl sequencing (WEM-seq) of clinical ESCC tissues and matched normal adjacent tissues, integrated with public microarray repositories. Following a rigorous dual-filter strategy to eliminate normal blood background noise, two hypermethylated loci, CACNA1E and SNTG1, were prioritized. A targeted quantitative methylation-specific PCR (qMSP) assay was developed and evaluated in a plasma cohort of 355 individuals (215 ESCC patients across stages 0-IV and 140 healthy controls). Five independent ESCC patient-derived organoid (PDO) models were established to investigate the mechanistic coupling between promoter hypermethylation and transcriptional silencing through paired qMSP and RNA sequencing. The CACNA1E/SNTG1 dual-marker cfDNA panel demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy. In the independent validation cohort, the combined classifier discriminated ESCC from healthy controls with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.918, yielding an optimal sensitivity of 90.5% and a specificity of 85.7%. For early-stage (Stage 0-I) ESCC, the panel maintained a highly robust AUC of 0.950 with 90.0% sensitivity and 87.5% specificity. In the PDO models, Actin-normalized qMSP analysis revealed intense promoter hypermethylation at CACNA1E and SNTG1, which strictly correlated with profound transcript depletion, providing direct in situ evidence of methylation-mediated gene silencing. The CACNA1E/SNTG1 methylation panel, combined with a qMSP workflow, provides a highly sensitive and specific strategy for the non-invasive early detection of ESCC. The integration of PDO-based multi-omics validation confirms the biological relevance of these epigenetic alterations, supporting the panel's broad utility for scalable clinical screening programs.

records.title: Single-Cell Whole-Transcriptome Detection Expands the Observable RNA Space for AI Virtual-Cell Models.
records.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing has supplied cell atlases and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled virtual-cell models with scalable, gene-level descriptions of cellular state. Yet prevalent poly(A)-based counting assays capture only part of the RNA landscape. Here, "single-cell whole-transcriptome detection" denotes sequencing-based efforts to detect a broader range of RNA biotypes than conventional poly(A)-based gene counting; no assay detects or quantifies every cellular RNA species without bias. We compare RNA-capture scope, transcript-structure resolution, temporal labeling, spatial context, and additional modalities as distinct measurement dimensions. From a biosensing perspective, analytical sensitivity, transcript coverage, throughput, and assay bias determine which signals are available to computational models. We then examine cell-state representations, regulatory networks, dynamics, perturbation prediction, and foundation models. Total-RNA assays reveal additional non-coding RNAs, long-read methods inform transcript structure, and temporal assays constrain RNA kinetics. Whether these signals improve prediction beyond conventional gene-count inputs requires matched, task-specific model comparisons. We distinguish molecular observability, statistical association, predictive performance, and causal validation, which requires appropriate interventions. We propose benchmarks controlling sequencing depth, cost, model architecture, and held-out samples while testing feature ablations, out-of-distribution performance, uncertainty calibration, and experimental outcomes. Together, high-throughput poly(A)-based profiling and broader RNA measurements provide complementary cellular breadth and regulatory depth.

records.title: Virtual cells: progress and challenges from mechanistic modeling to data-driven integration.
records.abstract: Virtual cells aim to represent cellular states computationally and predict responses to genetic, chemical, environmental, temporal, and spatial conditions. For comparative purposes, this review uses state encoding (E), state transition (T), and observation decoding (D) as a conceptual abstraction spanning explicit mechanistic models, data-driven foundation and perturbation models, multimodal systems, and spatial and multiscale simulation. We examine model boundaries, data foundations, resource disclosure, out-of-distribution evaluation, causal evidence, and experimental validation. Independent benchmarks show that parameter count and training-set size do not automatically yield robust out-of-distribution generalization, while transcriptomic representations alone do not capture the full functional state of a cell. Trustworthy virtual cells will require perturbation-responsive transitions, cross-modal alignment, continuous-time dynamics, mechanistic constraints, calibrated uncertainty, independent experimental validation, and, where appropriate, closed-loop experimental feedback.

records.title: Progress of metabolomics-centric multi-omics research in medicine.
records.abstract: Metabolomics reveals molecular changes at the metabolic level during biological processes. Recent advancements, particularly through integration with other omics and artificial intelligence (AI), are advancing metabolic data analysis and multi-omics interpretation. This review introduces a "metabolomics-centric" paradigm as a conceptual framework for multi-omics integration, positioning metabolic readouts as the functional anchor for interpreting genotype-phenotype relationships. It also chronicles the evolution and medical applications of integration technologies. Our discussion first traces the field's evolution from bulk to single-cell and spatial methodologies, next surveys integration strategies to uncover mechanistic insights, and finally examines how AI-driven multimodal data integration and AI-optimized metabolomics workflows tackle persistent biological and computational challenges. Looking forward, this review identifies the AI virtual cell as a pivotal future direction for metabolomics-based multi-omics integration, calling for increased attention to its development to simulate dynamic molecular phenotypic networks within a multi-omics context.

records.title: Emerging frontiers for AI in single-cell genomics.
records.abstract: We are just over a decade into the single-cell revolution in biology, which has been coupled to the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in single-cell genomics. Most early single-cell RNA embedding models and subsequent "foundation models"-representational models pretrained on large single-cell datasets-did not gain wide traction among experimental biologists. However, as massive single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) atlas efforts ramp up, there is a clear rationale for exploiting AI models to interpret new datasets in the context of vast existing data resources. Meanwhile, the advent of single-cell epigenetic/multiomic assays and Perturb-seq technologies presents new opportunities for AI modeling. Here, we review AI embedding and foundation models for scRNA-seq and single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (scATAC-seq), extensive machine-learning efforts to exploit single-cell multiome in regulatory genomics, and AI strategies to learn "virtual cell" models from Perturb-seq, ending with a description of current limitations of single-cell AI models and an outlook for future advances.

records.title: Benchmarking biological knowledge-graph priors against single-cell foundation models for Perturb-seq prediction.
records.abstract: Perturb-seq prediction increasingly relies on either biological graph priors or single-cell foundation models, but their relative value is difficult to interpret when architectures, split definitions and graph sources vary simultaneously. We benchmarked STRING functional associations and Gene Ontology co-annotation against dense, self-edge-only and exact-degree-rewired supports in one fixed graph-attention backbone, with a separate 200-HVG STRING-GO-control-co-expression sensitivity. Four public Perturb-seq datasets, three nested gene-space scales and three optimisation seeds were evaluated on held-out guide conditions; GEARS, scGPT and Geneformer were evaluated on the same held-out conditions, output-gene panels and Pearson-r metric after model-specific validity checks. At 200 highly variable genes, STRING-GO improved the equal-dataset Pearson r by +0.016 (95% interval [+0.010, +0.022]) relative to dense support. Dataset effects were positive in Adamson (+0.017), Norman (+0.015), Replogle K562 (+0.017) and Replogle RPE1 (+0.014), and 122/200 guide conditions improved (0.61 [0.54,0.68]). The top-20-gene Jaccard difference was +0.009 [+0.006,+0.012]. STRING-GO exceeded self-edge-only support by +0.024 [+0.018,+0.029] and the mean of ten exact-degree rewires by +0.011 [+0.005,+0.017]. The native-panel effect declined from +0.016 at 200 genes to +0.009 at 1000 genes; the 1000-200 interaction was -0.006 [-0.011,-0.002]. The primary graph-support comparison was formulated and conducted during peer-review revision rather than planned as an a priori confirmatory study. All three external models passed implementation-specific checks. Across 36 protocol-matched dataset-scale contrasts, 32 were within the descriptive ±0.030 reference envelope and four were outside, all favouring the external model. These results demonstrate a modest empirical predictive improvement under the evaluated matched protocol; they do not by themselves establish practical biological relevance.

records.title: AI-enabled fungal biomanufacturing: from genome mining to the artificial intelligence virtual cell.
records.abstract: Fungi are important chassis organisms for sustainable biomanufacturing owing to their strong secretion capacity, metabolic diversity, and adaptability to industrial processes. Driven by the rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI), computational approaches that enable machines to learn patterns from data and make predictions, together with omics technologies and synthetic biology, data- and model-driven strategies are increasingly reshaping fungal cell factory design and optimization. This review summarizes recent advances in AI-enabled fungal biomanufacturing, covering AI-assisted genome mining, enzyme and pathway analysis, genome editing, metabolic network modeling, and intelligent fermentation control. The review further highlights the emerging concept of the artificial intelligence virtual cell (AIVC), which integrates multi-omics data, mechanistic modeling, and machine learning-based approaches into a unified multiscale framework for simulating dynamic cellular behaviors. The technical foundations and potential applications of AIVC in fungal metabolic engineering, drug discovery, agriculture, and environmental biotechnology are reviewed. Finally, key challenges-data quality and standardization, cross-scale model integration and interpretability, and the gap between in silico prediction and experimental validation-are highlighted. This review provides a systematic perspective on the role of AI and virtual cell technologies in advancing next generation fungal biotechnology.

records.title: DRAGON-3D: an electron-density-aware generative model for dual-target drug molecule generation.
records.abstract: Dual-target drug molecule generation is a significant computational challenge due to the structural constraints imposed by two protein binding pockets. Existing generative models typically rely on scarce dual-target drug datasets and struggle to capture three-dimensional (3D) structural and physicochemical interactions between protein pockets and ligands, limiting generalization to new target pairs. To address these limitations, we propose DRAGON-3D, a general dual-target drug molecule generation model based on latent-space fusion of 3D electron-density representations of diverse target pairs. Our model employs a novel bi-Net β-VAE architecture and an innovative dual-pretraining strategy, enabling dual-target molecule generation using only single-target data. By integrating 3D spatial electron-density with 2D molecular topology, DRAGON-3D enhances generalization and spatial compatibility across diverse dual-target protein pairs. Comprehensive benchmarks show that DRAGON-3D is a promising framework for the generation of candidate dual-target molecules, particularly in molecular diversity, drug-likeness (QED), deployability, generalizability, and interpretability. Overall, DRAGON-3D provides an efficient, interpretable, and electron-density-informed paradigm for de novo dual-target molecular generation.

records.title: Shared α-helix chimeraffibodies enable linker-free bispecific protein design.
records.abstract: Small protein scaffolds enable precise targeting but often rely on flexible linkers that increase conformational heterogeneity and immunogenic liabilities. Here we develop Chimeraffibodies (CABs), a linker-free bispecific scaffold class that encodes interdomain geometry through seamless α-helix sharing. CABs are designed by AlphaSync, a structure-design framework that defines domain orientation through closed-form exhaustive local rigid-body superposition and ProteinMPNN-based sequence refinement. Using HER2-binding affibody and an albumin-binding domain, we generated 861CM, which preserved parental paratopes while enforcing a defined shared-helix architecture. Structural, biophysical and cellular analyses demonstrated stable assembly, cooperative target recruitment and retained affinity, with HSA binding of ∼14.3 pM and HER2 binding of 610 pM in the albumin-bound state. In vivo imaging revealed sustained tumor localization, reduced hepatic and renal background and improved organ-to-tumor contrast. CABs establish helix sharing as a geometry-encoded strategy for generating compact, homogeneous, and pharmacokinetically optimized bispecific proteins.

records.title: EquiDesign: a versatile computational framework for de novo protein sequence design.
records.abstract: Designing amino acid sequences that uniquely fold into target three-dimensional conformations defines the protein inverse folding problem, a formidable bottleneck in de novo protein design. Current computational paradigms, including deep learning-based approaches, often struggle to reconcile high sequence accuracy with structural stability, computational efficiency, and generalizability across diverse protein families. Here, we present EquiDesign, a deep learning framework that surmounts these constraints via a novel multistep Equiformer-enhanced architecture. By disentangling geometric features into invariant scalars and equivariant vectors, EquiDesign preserves the intrinsic directional topology of the protein backbone during message passing. This is achieved through spatial K-nearest neighbor graph construction and geometric attention mechanisms that hierarchically fuse multiscale contextual information, yielding a physically grounded representation of protein conformations. Extensive benchmarking demonstrates that EquiDesign achieves superior sequence recovery on standard and challenging test sets compared with state-of-the-art methods. Critically, the generated sequences exhibit exceptional structural fidelity, folding stability, and sequence diversity, as validated by comprehensive controls against training-set memorization, compositional bias, and physical energy landscapes, alongside targeted diversity sampling. These results establish EquiDesign as a robust, scalable, and generalizable inverse folding solution, driven by SE(3)-equivariant encoding and multiscale geometric attention, thus propelling de novo protein design toward unprecedented structural precision.

records.title: Building a Physically Interpretable Compressed Chemical Space via Grid-Based Optimization.
records.abstract: In recent years, deep generative models have been increasingly adopted for molecular optimization and design. In many such models, molecules are encoded into latent spaces that provide compact representations of their features. However, these latent spaces remain difficult to interpret in physical terms, and it is unclear how much structural and molecular information is retained under compression. This limitation becomes especially important when molecular behavior depends on specific three-dimensional arrangements embedded in an environmental context. Here, we introduce COMPRESS (Compression Of Molecular Physical fields into Reduced Spatial Sites), an optimization framework that represents a small molecule using a fixed number of physically parametrized spatial sites. Each site is defined by three spatial coordinates and three interaction parameters, yielding a fixed-size representation that remains directly interpretable in physical terms. To preserve molecular information, COMPRESS representations are optimized to reproduce the density, electrostatic, and van der Waals fields of the corresponding all-atom molecule on discretized three-dimensional grids. We systematically evaluate how molecular information is retained as the number of sites, K, is reduced. Our analysis covers benzene, 20 chemically diverse chemical scaffolds, benzene dimers, protein-ligand complexes, and 10,000 molecules chosen from the GEOM-Drugs data set. Across systems, field agreement deteriorates slowly at high resolution and then undergoes a rapid, pronounced transition at lower resolution. We further find that K = 25 conformers capture about 97% of the molecules from GEOM-Drugs under a loss threshold of 0.05, which we use as an indicator of fidelity. These results show that COMPRESS can provide a fixed-size, physically interpretable molecular representation, enabling compression to be evaluated directly using molecular interaction fields and resulting physical quantities. We also introduce a decoder that reconstructs all-atom structures directly from a COMPRESS representation, showing that the representation can support molecular generation in addition to field-preservation analysis. Finally, rationally modified COMPRESS representations through changes to site charge and size or the addition or removal of sites are shown to generate realistic chemical compounds upon decoding.

records.title: Programming N-linked glycan composition through de novo protein design.
records.abstract: N-linked glycans are ubiquitous post-translational modifications that mediate diverse biological processes, including cell signaling and adhesion, molecular recognition, and host-pathogen interactions. Despite their importance, N-linked glycans have largely remained beyond the reach of biomolecular design due to a lack of methods capable of jointly modeling glycans and protein structure. Here, we develop a general all-atom computational pipeline for creating de novo glycoproteins in which the amino acid sequence encodes both the location and composition of N-linked glycans. The method uses three-dimensional protein structure to tune glycan accessibility to processing enzymes in the eukaryotic secretory pathway. Systematic increases in steric restriction progressively reduced processing, shifting glycans from heterogeneous complex-type structures toward increasingly underprocessed oligomannose-type species resembling those found on many viral glycoproteins. Despite this programmed restriction, the resulting oligomannose glycans remained accessible for biological recognition, inhibiting uropathogenic Escherichia coli adhesion to human bladder cells and binding mannose-binding lectin. These results establish steric control of N-glycan processing as a genetically encodable design principle and extend computational protein design to functional glycoproteins with programmed composition.

records.title: The physical foundation beneath protein generative modeling.
records.abstract: Physical equations in protein modeling appear to have been replaced by generative models trained directly on structure data. By learning a mapping from noise to data, sampling de novo protein structures has become much more efficient. However, such models can also learn non-physical features and break down with out-of-distribution settings which are typical in protein design campaigns. In this review, we highlight where the physics persists in protein generative modeling pipelines and the issues that linger when physically relevant components of a macromolecular system are left unmodeled. We present a perspective that respecting the underlying physics of macromolecular systems, increasingly through learned representations that are physically grounded and updating generative models with experimental data, is foundational to generative modeling for functional protein design.

records.title: Temperature-Resolved Coding for Highly Multiplexed Digital PCR Using MeltArray.
records.abstract: Digital PCR enables sensitive absolute nucleic acid quantification, but its broader application remains constrained by limited multiplexing capacity. Here we report digital MeltArray (dMeltArray), a temperature-resolved endpoint decoding strategy that transfers MeltArray mediator-probe chemistry to a static droplet-imaging digital PCR system. In dMeltArray, target-specific mediator products generate fluorescent reporter duplexes with programmed melting temperatures. Post-amplification imaging at discrete temperatures progressively erases lower-Tm signals while retaining higher-Tm signals, allowing target-specific concentrations to be recovered from Poisson-corrected cumulative counts within each fluorescence channel. This strategy converts melting temperature into a programmable readout dimension requiring no real-time tracking or full-curve acquisition, addressing key trade-offs between multiplexing capacity, workflow simplicity, and cost. dMeltArray can be combined with 5'-hydrolysis probes, adding an orthogonal persistent-signal readout in the same optical framework. As proof-of-concept applications, we developed a 13-plex assay for post-transplantation viruses, an 11-plex assay for KRAS/BRAF hotspot mutations, and a 14-plex assay that integrates a 5'-hydrolysis probe into the 13-plex panel. These findings establish temperature-resolved endpoint decoding as a scalable route to multiplex digital PCR and support multidimensional target encoding by combining spectral, thermal and hydrolysis-probe readouts without requiring full melting-curve acquisition.

records.title: Arteriovenous Malformations as Neoplastic-Like Lesions: Molecular Underpinnings and Implications for the Interventional Radiologist.
records.abstract: Arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) are high-flow vascular anomalies traditionally treated as congenital structural lesions with embolization or surgical resection. However, recurrence after embolization alone exceeds 90%, underscoring incomplete understanding of their biology. Next-generation sequencing has identified somatic gain-of-function mutations in KRAS, MAP2K1, BRAF, and HRAS as drivers of sporadic AVMs. Confined to lesional endothelial cells, these mutations activate RAS/MAPK signaling and support a neoplastic-like rather than purely structural disease model. This has therapeutic implications: MEK inhibitors, particularly trametinib, have shown angiographic and clinical responses in refractory AVMs. Interventional radiologists can obtain draining vein liquid-biopsy samples during embolization for molecular genotyping; embolization may increase circulating cell-free DNA yield. This review summarizes the molecular rationale, targeted therapy evidence, and integration of genotyping into embolization workflows to enable combined treatment strategies.Level of Evidence: No level of evidence assigned (Review Article).

records.title: Self-aggregated photo-heterostructures enhancing fluorescence for cancer diagnosis and treatment monitoring.
records.abstract: Semiconductor zinc oxide (ZnO) nanostructures as classic photonic materials have sparked the development of low-cost, high-performance fluorescence sensors; however, their scalable clinical applications remain hampered by inadequate sensitivity. Here, we engineer a high-curvature photo-heterostructure aggregate-enhanced fluorescence (PAEF) sensor based on bubble-scaffolded ZnO nanorods. Leveraging synergistic evanescent field coupling and self-aggregation of photo-heterostructures, PAEF sensor streamlines efficient isolation (~90%) and ultrasensitive profiling of tumor extracellular vesicles (EVs) in a single assay, achieving sensitivity <10 EVs/μL (104-fold better than ELISA) without additional amplification, outperforming most state-of-the-art EV fluorescence assays. This self-sufficient sensor enables accurate monitoring of targeted therapeutic efficacy in mouse xenograft models via simultaneous dual-marker readout. We further show its clinical utility in hepatocellular carcinoma diagnosis with ≥96% accuracy (≥98% specificity) in two cohorts (n = 146), improving dynamic monitoring of surgical treatment responses, particularly in alpha-fetoprotein-negative patients. This work provides a cost-effective ultrasensitive liquid biopsy tool advancing non-invasive cancer diagnosis.

records.title: [Genomic alterations in thymic epithelial tumors: State of knowledge, and the interest of liquid biopsy].
records.abstract: In the absence of randomized phase III trial data, thymic epithelial tumors (TETs) are rare malignancies of the prevascular mediastinum managed according to the WHO histological and the Masaoka-Koga classifications. Next-generation sequencing has revealed distinct mutational characteristics between thymomas, which are characterized by a low tumor mutational burden and a near-specific GTF2I mutation, and thymic carcinomas which are dominated by alterations in CDKN2A, TP53 and KIT. These findings open the way for novel therapeutic strategies, involving immune checkpoint inhibitors and multi-kinase inhibitors in advanced thymic carcinomas. Notwithstanding the potential of liquid biopsy as a non-invasive monitoring tool, specific biological obstacles in TETs currently limit its clinical applicability. Recent confirmation of the interest of liquid biopsy in perioperative management of lung cancer raises the prospect of transferring this approach to TETs. The key challenge lies in identifying the biological marker most suited to the monitoring of longitudinal tumors. Genomic profiling of TETs enhances (rather than supplants) the historical histological classification, and should progressively inform therapeutic stratification, particularly in cases of thymic carcinoma.

records.title: Intersection Rules Subtest Timing as a Predictor of DriveSafe DriveAware Outcomes: A Pilot Study.
records.abstract: ImportanceIntersection Rules Subtest timing is a potential predictor of the DriveSafe outcome score in DriveSafe DriveAware (DSDA) assessment.ObjectiveTo examine whether Intersection Rules completion time is associated with DriveSafe outcome within the DSDA assessment.DesignRetrospective, observational pilot study using secondary data.SettingAustralian metropolitan fitness-to-drive clinic.ParticipantsOf 169 participants (median age = 80; 61.5% male), 104 categorised into non-pass group of DriveSafe subtest formed 'cases', whilst 65 who passed were 'controls'.Outcomes and MeasuresPrimary predictor: Intersection Rules Subtest completion time in seconds. Primary outcome: DriveSafe subtest outcome, categorised as pass/non-pass. Relationships analysed using logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.ResultsLonger Intersection Rules Subtest time significantly predicted lower DriveSafe subtest outcome (non-pass) scores, with each additional 60 s increasing odds of failure by 93.7% (odds ratio [OR] = 1.94, 95% confidence interval [CI] [1.40, 2.68], p < .001). A ROC curve analysis revealed an area under the curve of 0.73 (95% CI: [.654, .807]). An optimal cut-off of 213.5 s showed high specificity (86.2%) (95% CI: [75.3, 93.5]) but modest sensitivity (48.1%) (95% CI: [38.2, 58.1]) for a non-pass result.Conclusions and RelevanceIntersection Rules Subtest completion time was associated with DriveSafe outcome in this pilot study. The current findings support future study of this timing metric, which may have potential as a clinical decision-support indicator, a 'Detect and Pause' step, after prospective validation and DSDA protocol sequence modification.
